messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj is a 58-year-old South Asian male who works as a product manager and has been married for over three decades. His life took a dark turn several years ago when he was subjected to torture while visiting family in his home country. The trauma of this experience continues to affect his daily life, manifesting in various ways that have strained both his professional and personal relationships. Raj had come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that there is something inherently wrong with him that made the event happen. These negative appraisals led him to adopt maladaptive strategies to cope with his trauma. He avoids anything that could be stressful, constantly checks his body for signs of danger or injury, and stays away from military uniforms or weapons, which remind him of his torturers. The mistrust he developed after the traumatic event has made Raj hyper-vigilant about his safety. He reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly, even in familiar settings such as at home or at work. This constant state of alertness makes it nearly impossible for him to relax, even in safe environments. At night, Raj wakes up frequently to check if he is still safe, a behavior that has only reinforced his negative beliefs about the world and himself. Raj's hyper-vigilance and mistrust have led to a cycle where his threat perceptions are exacerbated by his maladaptive strategies. For instance, his constant monitoring of his body for signs of danger fuels his sense of unease and makes him more sensitive to triggers like incomprehensible chatter or sirens, which often remind him of the chaos he experienced during torture. In his role as a product manager, Raj has found that his avoidance behaviors have impacted his ability to function effectively. Meetings with colleagues can be particularly challenging, especially when there is background noise from other conversations or discussions about work-related stressors. He finds himself leaving meetings early or avoiding them altogether, which has led to misunderstandings and strained professional relationships. Raj’s belief in his intrinsic fault has also affected his personal life. His wife often feels distant as Raj struggles to engage in normal activities together without feeling anxious or triggered. For instance, a routine trip to the mall can be fraught with anxiety due to the ambient noise and the possibility of encountering sirens from emergency vehicles. Over time, this cycle of mistrust and maladaptive coping has deepened Raj’s negative appraisals. He increasingly believes that nothing good can happen to him anymore, which further reinforces his avoidance behaviors and perpetuates a sense of threat even in benign situations. This loop is particularly evident when he experiences dizziness or lightheadedness, interpreting these sensations as signs of impending danger rather than benign physical symptoms. The tipping point for Raj came recently when an unexpected touch from a colleague at work caused him to react with such alarm that it led to a panic attack in front of the team. This incident was a stark reminder of his ongoing struggle and marked the moment he realized he needed help. Despite his fears, Raj is hoping that therapy can provide relief from the constant state of vigilance and help him rebuild trust in others. Raj’s current state is one of profound distress and isolation. He is most afraid of reliving the trauma or being triggered by everyday sounds and sensations that remind him of torture. At the same time, he hopes for a sense of safety and normalcy in his daily life, free from the constant fear and hyper-vigilance that have become his norm.
